name: Apitherapy

lead: Apitherapy is a branch of complementary medicine that uses products from honeybees: honey, propolis, bee pollen, royal jelly, beeswax and bee venom. Practitioners apply or ingest them, and venom is delivered by stings or injections.

For appearance, the relevant uses are skin-focused: honey and propolis in wound and skin care, and bee products studied in skin conditions such as plaque psoriasis. Reviews of the field describe most evidence as laboratory-based or small trials, and Wikipedia states there is no clinical evidence for the efficacy or safety of apitherapy treatments.

paras: People use topical honey or propolis preparations, take royal jelly, pollen or propolis as supplements, or, in venom therapy, receive controlled stings or injected venom from a practitioner. A trial in plaque psoriasis injected bee venom into lesions weekly for up to 12 treatments.

Bee venom can cause reactions from local swelling to anaphylaxis, and frequent exposure has been linked to joint damage. A 55-year-old woman died in 2018 after live bee acupuncture. People allergic to bee products, pollen or stings are at particular risk, and allergy testing is advised in clinical descriptions of the practice.

angle.text: People use honey, propolis, royal jelly and venom-based treatments in the hope of calmer, healthier skin. Evidence comes from small trials and laboratory work.

lead: Apitherapy is the therapeutic use of honeybee products: honey, propolis, bee pollen and bee bread, royal jelly, beeswax and bee venom (apitoxin) [1][2]. Its proponents date it to ancient Egypt, Greece and China, and Wikipedia traces modern bee venom therapy to Austrian physician Philipp Terc's 1888 article and the term to Hungarian physician Bodog Beck in 1935 [2].

Its place in an appearance-focused wiki is mainly through the skin. Honey and propolis are used in wound and skin care, royal jelly appears in cosmetics and supplements, and bee venom has been studied as an injected treatment for plaque psoriasis [1][3]. Practitioners also claim benefit in eczema, arthritis and other conditions [2].

Research is described as largely preclinical or small-scale, and Wikipedia states that apitherapy has no clinical evidence of efficacy or safety [2]. Reviews describe bee venom components such as melittin as having anti-inflammatory activity in the laboratory [4].
infobox: Honey, propolis, pollen, royal jelly, beeswax, venom [1]

paras: Honey is a sugar-rich solution with enzymes and antioxidants; its antibacterial properties are attributed to high osmotic pressure, low pH and hydrogen peroxide formation [1]. Propolis is a resin collected by bees from plants and contains flavonoids and phenolic acids [1]. Royal jelly is a secretion that feeds queen larvae and contains proteins and the fatty acid 10-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid [1][5]. Bee venom is a mixture dominated by peptides such as melittin [1][4].

Skin conditions are among the claimed targets of apitherapy, including eczema and psoriasis [2]. In a randomised double-blind trial of 50 patients with recalcitrant localised plaque psoriasis, bee venom or placebo was injected into lesions weekly for up to 12 treatments, with follow-up at six months and measurement of serum TNF-alpha [6]. A 2026 randomised trial examined local bee products for nappy dermatitis in infants [7]. A trial of royal jelly with green propolis in haemodialysis patients examined cardiovascular risk markers rather than appearance [8].

Adverse reactions to bee venom therapy are frequent, and sensitised people can experience reactions from local swelling to anaphylaxis or death [2]. Frequent venom exposure can cause arthropathy [2]. In 2018 a 55-year-old woman died after live bee acupuncture, and researchers called the therapy unsafe [2]. A review of allergens in Korea notes that bee venom allergy has been linked to apitherapy in traditional medicine [9].

Human trials exist for specific uses: the plaque psoriasis injection trial [6], a haemodialysis supplement trial [8] and a 2026 nappy dermatitis trial [7]. Reviews cover osteoarthritis [10] and menopausal symptoms [11], and Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence for efficacy or safety of apitherapy overall [2]. Venom and honey work in cancer is described in reviews as laboratory and early-stage research [4][12].
